questions.q: What is the real trade-off in choosing a spread width?
options: A wider spread earns more per trade but fills less often and reduces adverse-selection risk; a narrower spread fills more often but earns less and raises adverse-selection risk
Wider spreads always produce more total profit with no downside
Spread width has no effect on fill frequency
Narrower spreads always reduce adverse-selection risk
questions.explain: Spread width is a genuine trade-off, not a dial to maximize in one direction -- wider earns more per fill but gets hit less often; narrower fills more but raises adverse-selection exposure.

questions.q: In the lesson's simplified spread-sizing function, what two things determine the final spread?
options: A risk-based spread (scaling with volatility and risk aversion) and a competitive floor -- whichever is larger wins
Only volatility, with no other factor considered
Only the competitive floor, with volatility ignored
A fixed constant that never changes regardless of market conditions
questions.explain: The function takes the max of the risk-based spread and the competitive floor -- ensuring the spread never gets too tight to compensate for risk, nor too wide to actually get filled against competition.

questions.q: Why is reservation-price skewing alone not a sufficient risk control, according to this lesson?
options: It's a probabilistic nudge, not a guarantee -- in a one-sided/trending market, a maker can keep getting filled on one side regardless of how skewed its quotes are, since skew only changes relative competitiveness, not whether a counterparty shows up
Reservation-price skewing only works for options, not equities
Reservation-price skewing is mathematically guaranteed to prevent all inventory growth
Reservation-price skewing requires a hard inventory limit to even function at all
questions.explain: Skewing changes the odds, not the certainty -- in persistent one-sided markets, a maker can still accumulate inventory beyond what the risk parameter was tuned to tolerate, which is exactly why a hard backstop is needed.

questions.q: What makes a hard inventory limit a genuinely different mechanism from reservation-price skewing?
options: It's a hard rule that triggers direct action at a threshold, not a probabilistic nudge that only changes relative quote competitiveness
They are actually the same mechanism, just described differently
Inventory limits only apply to short positions, never long ones
Inventory limits replace the need for a fair-value estimate entirely
questions.explain: A hard limit takes explicit action (suppressing a side, widening aggressively, or actively crossing the spread) once a threshold is reached -- a fundamentally different kind of control than a soft, probabilistic skew.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say gamma, spread width, and inventory limit should be tuned together, not independently?
options: A maker running a wider spread and higher gamma can often tolerate a higher inventory limit, since each fill already carries more compensation and the reservation price already works harder to prevent extreme positions
These three parameters have no relationship to each other at all
Only gamma matters; spread width and inventory limit are purely cosmetic settings
Tuning them together is impossible with real fill data
questions.explain: The three parameters interact -- a higher gamma and wider spread both reduce the practical need for a very tight inventory limit, so treating them as independent dials misses how they actually work together as one system.
